scenes.text: Ever broken a website and wished you could just hit undo? That's exactly what GitHub is for.
It starts with version control. A tool called Git saves a snapshot of your code every time you make a change. That snapshot is a commit.
Each commit is a point in history, so you can see who changed what, and when.
A repository, or repo, is your project folder plus that whole history. GitHub keeps it safe in the cloud.
Laptop died? No problem. Your code is backed up on GitHub, ready to download again.
Pushed a bug to the live site? Roll back to yesterday's working commit in seconds.
Cloning copies the whole repo to any computer with one command. New laptop, new teammate, same project.
Want to try a new feature? Create a branch. It's a safe copy where you can experiment without touching the live site.
When it's ready, open a pull request. Teammates review the changes, leave comments, then merge it into main.
That's how many developers build one website at the same time, without overwriting each other's work.
Commit, push, branch, merge. Learn GitHub once, and every client project gets safer. Follow for more.
